statement: When we know xt and NG⋆ (xt ), we actually have full information feedback (i.e., we can compute the prediction of every hypothesis ourselves). Hence, we can apply the realizable-to-agnostic technique by constructing a cover of H with T M experts, where M is the mistake bound in the realizable setting, and then running multiplicative weights over these experts. For the construction of the experts, we apply the same method by Ben-David et al. (2009). The only minor difference is that the learner in our setting needs to produce a hypothesis at each round to induce some labeling instead of deciding a labeling directly. Given the hypothesis e ht generated by a realizable algorithm AREL , to flip the prediction induced by e ht , we can change the entire neighborhood of xt to negative if e ht ’s prediction is positive, and predict xt by positive if e ht ’s prediction is negative. If we do not know (xt , NG⋆ (xt )), then we do not even know how to flip the prediction.
